sections.markdown:
**Think of `webview_flutter` as embedding a mini Chrome browser tab inside your Flutter widget.**

Some content — help articles, OAuth flows, third-party checkout pages, existing web dashboards — is easier to render as HTML than to rebuild in Flutter. WebView lets you drop that in as a native view.

- **Native browser engine** — Android uses **WebView (Chromium via Play Services)**, iOS uses **WKWebView** (Safari's engine). Not Flutter's Skia — it's a PlatformView.
- **JavaScript channels** — post messages between JS ↔ Dart in both directions.
- **Navigation delegate** — intercept URL loads: block, redirect, open in system browser.
- **Cookies + storage** — separate from your app's HTTP client; be aware for auth flows.
- **Progress + title events** — hook the loading UI.
- **Local HTML** — `loadHtmlString` for embedded content (bundled help pages).

**Why every Flutter app inevitably needs it:** third-party OAuth (Google / Facebook / Twitter often), Stripe / Razorpay checkouts, WordPress-backed help content, legacy web admin dashboards. Building all of that natively is impossible. WebView is the escape hatch. **The trap:** it's a full browser inside your app — permission surfaces, cookie management, security implications.

**`webview_flutter`** (`^4.x`) is the Flutter team's official WebView plugin. Renders a native browser view: `WebView` on Android (Play Services WebView, Chromium-based), `WKWebView` on iOS. Federated architecture — `webview_flutter_android` + `webview_flutter_wkwebview` + `webview_flutter_web`. API: `WebViewController.load*`, `runJavaScript`, `addJavaScriptChannel`, `setNavigationDelegate`, cookie manager, storage manager.

## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: Trusting JS in the WebView.** ANY code you `runJavaScript` executes with the page's origin. Never inject secrets or auth tokens into a WebView you don't fully control.
**Mistake 2: Loading `http://` URLs.** Both platforms block by default. Configure allowances in AndroidManifest / Info.plist only when truly necessary; prefer https.
**Mistake 3: JS channel messages are strings.** JSON-encode/decode manually. A big binary through the channel = slow + memory intensive.
**Mistake 4: External links opening inside the WebView.** Users get stuck. Add a `NavigationDelegate` that punts non-matching hosts to `launchUrl`.

**Mistake 5: Cookie sharing surprises.** WebView cookies are SEPARATE from Dio's cookie jar. OAuth done in a WebView won't naturally propagate to your API client — use post-redirect + capture the token.
**Mistake 6: Not disposing.** WebViewController may hold a native handle; leaks contribute to memory pressure. `initState` construct + rely on Flutter's widget lifecycle.
**Mistake 7: Blindly enabling `unrestricted` JavaScript.** OK for trusted content, dangerous for arbitrary URLs. Set `disabled` for static HTML docs.
**Mistake 8: Assuming WebView === real browser.** Missing APIs (some Payment Request, some device APIs), different user agents, older engines on some Android devices.
## Best practices
**1. HTTPS only.** Reject mixed content.
**2. NavigationDelegate whitelists** — only your domain loads inside; else external browser.
**3. JS channels JSON-encoded** for structured data.
**4. Progress bar** at top for UX.
**5. Test on Play Services & non-GMS Android** — WebView engine varies.
**6. `WebViewCookieManager` for auth cookies** if you MUST share state.
**7. `clearLocalStorage` on logout.**
**8. `flutter_inappwebview` alternative** — more features + control if you outgrow `webview_flutter`.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — Load a help URL + progress bar.
**Practice 2 (Medium)** — NavigationDelegate opens external links via system browser.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — JS channel: page dispatches 'close' → Flutter pops route.

## Interview Q&A

**Q1: When do you use a WebView vs building the screen in Flutter?**

**A:** WebView when: **(1) Content lives on the web** — WordPress-backed help articles, marketing pages that Product wants to iterate on without a release, blog posts. **(2) Third-party flows** — OAuth (Google, Facebook), Stripe / Razorpay checkout, KYC providers, insurance/banking widgets. **(3) Complex existing web UI** — internal admin dashboard reused inside the app during migration. **Not a WebView when:** the screen is core to the app UX (branded, high-frequency), animations matter, offline required, small deep-linking / user-flow needs. **Cost of WebView:** slower cold-start (browser boot), different UX language (scroll/tap feel differs), cookie/session isolation, third-party trust surface. **Rule:** WebView is an escape hatch, not the default UI framework.

**Q2: How do JavaScript channels work + when to use them?**

**A:** `addJavaScriptChannel('Flutter', onMessageReceived: (msg) { ... })` injects a `window.Flutter` object into the loaded page. JS calls `Flutter.postMessage(str)`; the string arrives in Dart's callback. **Dart → JS:** `controller.runJavaScript('...')` executes arbitrary JS. **Use cases:** (1) The web page signals 'user closed the flow'; Flutter pops. (2) Web page needs a native feature (open camera, close dialog) — post an action string, Flutter handles + optionally posts back via runJavaScript. (3) Deep integration with a hosted checkout — post payment result → Flutter processes. **Caveats:** messages are STRINGS — JSON-encode structured data. **Security:** you injected `Flutter` into the page's global scope — a compromised/hostile page can now call it. Only add channels for pages you fully control.

**Q3: How do you handle OAuth flows inside a WebView?**

**A:** **Classic pattern:** Provider (Google/Facebook) hosts a login page; on success, redirects to your `redirect_uri` with an auth code in the query string. **Steps:** (1) Load the provider's auth URL in the WebView. (2) `NavigationDelegate.onNavigationRequest` — inspect each nav. (3) When the URL matches your `redirect_uri`, extract the code from the query string. (4) `NavigationDecision.prevent` to stop the WebView loading it. (5) Exchange the code for a token via your backend (or PKCE-based direct exchange). (6) Pop the WebView, store token in `flutter_secure_storage`. **Modern alternative:** `flutter_web_auth_2` uses the platform's ASWebAuthenticationSession / Custom Tabs — better UX, cookies isolated correctly, no WebView view surface. **Recommend the modern path** whenever the provider supports it.

**Q4: What are the cookie / session isolation gotchas?**

**A:** The WebView has its OWN cookie jar + localStorage / sessionStorage — separate from your Flutter HTTP client's (Dio's). Consequence: (1) Logging into a website inside the WebView does NOT log Dio in. (2) API tokens sent by Dio don't appear in the WebView. (3) A logout must clear cookies in BOTH clients. **Sharing cookies:** `WebViewCookieManager().setCookie(WebViewCookie(name, value, domain))` to inject; read via `runJavaScript('document.cookie')`. **Complex flows** (SSO, shared session) — use `flutter_inappwebview` for finer cookie control, or move auth to a native SDK. **Logout:** `controller.clearCache() + WebViewCookieManager().clearCookies() + clearLocalStorage()`. Do the same on your Dio-side jar.

**Q5: How do you keep the WebView secure?**

**A:** **(1) HTTPS-only.** Reject `http://`. Android manifest: no `usesCleartextTraffic`; iOS Info.plist: no NSAllowsArbitraryLoads. **(2) Domain whitelist** via NavigationDelegate — non-whitelisted URLs redirected to system browser. **(3) Never inject secrets into the page.** Any script the page loads sees `window.*`. Only expose safe callbacks. **(4) `runJavaScript` audit** — treat the input as untrusted; escape user input. **(5) `disable` JS mode** for static HTML docs. **(6) `clearCache`/`clearLocalStorage` on logout.** **(7) File / camera access** — WebView asks permission separately; grant only when trusted. **(8) Mixed content** off. **(9) Content Security Policy** on served pages restricts what scripts can do. **(10) Update the WebView engine** — Android's WebView is auto-updated via Play Store, but non-GMS devices may be old. Interviewers respect the layered defense answer.

**Q6: When would you migrate to `flutter_inappwebview` instead?**

**A:** `flutter_inappwebview` is a community package with far more control: (1) Fine-grained cookie management (shared jar with a Dio interceptor). (2) Header injection per request. (3) Custom URL scheme handling. (4) Print / PDF export. (5) WebView pool for pre-warmed browsers. (6) Ad-blocking hooks. (7) Content blockers. **Cost:** more features = more API surface; slower to update to new Flutter versions. `webview_flutter` is the official minimal one — recommended for typical needs; `flutter_inappwebview` when you outgrow it. **Common migration triggers:** complex auth cookie sharing; injecting request headers; custom scheme intercepts for deep links; ad-block; PDF viewer. Interviewers score highly on 'pick the smaller tool by default; upgrade when there's a specific need.'

## Real-world usage

- **Help / support** — WordPress-backed articles.
- **Third-party checkout** — Stripe / Razorpay / PayPal.
- **OAuth (fallback)** — when native SDK isn't available; prefer `flutter_web_auth_2`.
- **Legacy admin dashboards** — during Flutter migration.
- **Terms + Privacy** — hosted HTML with easy updates.
- **NOT ideal for** — core UX screens; offline scenarios; animation-heavy content.

## Advanced notes

- **`loadFlutterAsset`** — bundled HTML/CSS/JS.
- **`WKWebViewConfiguration.mediaTypesRequiringUserAction`** — auto-play video.
- **`androidHardwareAcceleration`** — often needed for smooth scroll.
- **`onPageStarted` / `onPageFinished`** — analytics + loading state.
- **`onWebResourceError`** — log 404 / TLS failures.
- **`shouldOverrideUrlLoading` (inappwebview)** — deeper control.
- **PWA integration** — WebView can host a PWA; but background sync + push differ.
- **File download** — configure via `onDownloadStart` (inappwebview) or intercept navigation for cases like PDF.
- **`gestureRecognizers`** — resolve gesture conflicts with parent scroll.
- **Web target** — `webview_flutter_web` renders as an iframe; less feature-parity.
- **Debug** — remote debugging via `chrome://inspect` (Android) or Safari (iOS).
